processes.description: Each month a cost-allocation coordinator (Shari Mao, James Scribner, Suzanne Nicholie) sends the Hours Survey and Activity Survey with instructions, asking staff to enter hours and activities for the month just ended so the data can feed the cost and price model. A helper spreadsheet is offered; respondents fill in, resave and return the file by a stated deadline, and the coordinator checks returns against ATEs staffing and follows up. Separately, an assistant collects time reports and staff reply with the vacation, sick or holiday days they took.
steps: Coordinator sends the monthly Hours Survey and Activity Survey with instructions, or opens the survey for input.
Respondents gather their hours and the share of time spent per activity or commercial team, optionally in the helper spreadsheet.
Respondents fill in, resave and return the survey file by the stated deadline.
Coordinator sends deadline-day reminders and chases those who have not responded.
Coordinator checks returns against ATEs staffing records and queries discrepancies with the team.
Coordinator loads the collected data into the cost allocation model.
For timesheets, the assistant asks for time reports and staff reply with the vacation, sick or holiday days taken.

stalls.summary: Many respondents miss the survey deadline, so coordinators send reminders on the due date and after it has passed.
Surveys fall behind and are requested for several months at once, with later follow-ups asking staff which commercial team they supported and in what share.
Staffing reported for a team does not line up with the ATEs records, so the coordinator has to query the team before the data can be used.

automation.approach: Pre-fill each person's survey from timekeeping (ATEs) and the staff roster, collect it through one standard form that checks hours and allocations add up, send automatic reminders ahead of the deadline, and flag returns that disagree with ATEs before they are loaded into the model. Timesheet absences could be entered by staff directly rather than relayed to the assistant.
automation.rationale: The recurring effort is re-sending, filling in and reconciling the same survey layout every month. A single pre-filled survey template with built-in totals checks cuts the entry and reconciliation work and reduces late or inconsistent returns, while people still judge how their time splits across activities.

work_estimate.rationale: A round involves preparing the survey attachment and instructions, respondents looking up their hours and splitting them across activities or teams, filling in and resaving the file, and the coordinator checking returns against ATEs and loading them into the model. About 25 minutes mid; 10 when a round is only a timesheet absence entry, up to 60 when it includes reconciling staffing against ATEs. Pre-filling from timekeeping and automatic totals checks could take over much of the lookup and entry; the allocation judgement stays manual.

processes.description: Employees ask their manager (Bill Williams) for particular days off or a longer vacation. The manager replies approving the dates, telling staff to take the days and to give notice of longer vacations in advance as everyone else in the group does. The approved days are put down on the group's vacation calendar, and staff ask to be put down for further dates as needed.
steps: Employee emails the manager asking for particular days off or a vacation.
Manager checks the dates against the group's coverage and other planned absences.
Manager replies approving the days, asking for advance notice of longer vacations.
The approved dates are entered on the vacation calendar, and further dates are added on request.

automation.approach: A shared leave calendar with a short request form: the employee enters the dates, the manager sees overlapping absences and approves in one step, and approved dates land on the calendar without being re-keyed.
automation.rationale: The work is small and repetitive: checking overlap and recording dates. A standard request and calendar layout keeps approvals and the calendar in step, while the coverage decision stays with the manager.

work_estimate.rationale: Hands-on work is checking the requested dates against the group's coverage and recording them on the vacation calendar: about 3 minutes, as the approvals shown are brief; up to 10 when a longer vacation has to be fitted around others' plans. A shared request form feeding the calendar could take over the recording; the approval decision stays manual.

processes.description: When a trade has to be verified or a question with a counterparty is being worked through, someone on the trading or risk side asks for the recorded phone lines to be pulled for a named trader on a given date and time window, such as Geir's conversations in a late-afternoon window or Ryan Slinger's calls at two specific times. The tapes are retrieved and reviewed so the terms of the trade can be confirmed.
steps: A trade needing verification or in dispute is identified.
The requester pins down the trader, date and time window of the relevant calls.
The requester emails a request to have the tapes pulled for that trader and window.
The recordings are located and retrieved.
The calls are reviewed to confirm what was agreed and the finding is used to settle the trade.

stalls.summary: The same tape pull for Geir's conversations is first raised as probably needed and then restated in a separate message as still needed, so the request is carried across threads before it is acted on.

automation.approach: A standard tape request capturing trader, phone line, date, time window, deal reference and reason, sent to the recording group, together with a recording index searchable by trader and timestamp so the right calls can be found quickly.
automation.rationale: Requests are free-text and vary in how precisely they name the calls. A fixed request message makes every pull complete the first time and avoids restating the same request; listening to the calls and judging the trade remain manual.

work_estimate.rationale: Minutes go to identifying the trader and call times from the deal record, having the recordings located and retrieved, and listening through them to confirm the terms. About 30 minutes mid; 10 for a call at a known time, up to 90 when a window covering much of a late afternoon has to be reviewed. A request template and a searchable recording index could take over locating the calls; listening and judging stay manual.
